title: The Uganda martyrs (1886)
hookLine: Charles Lwanga and young companions, Catholic and Anglican, killed by a king

cards: The court of the Kabaka, the king of Buganda, on the shores of a great lake in East Africa. Young pages run messages, carry water, stand at the doors.

Some of them have been listening to newcomers: Catholic missionaries, and Anglican missionaries too. Some of the pages have been baptized, and they pray together in secret. The young king, Mwanga, grows angry and afraid.
He sees the new faith pulling his pages' loyalty somewhere he can't control, and they are refusing some of his demands. One day he orders the Christians at court to step forward. They step forward.

teach.b: First, the elder. Joseph Mukasa, a Catholic and a senior servant at court, had protected the pages and spoken honestly to the king. The king had him killed before the pages were taken.
Second, the leader of the pages.

Charles Lwanga took his place, looking after the young Christians. Tradition says that on the night before they were taken, he baptized some of the boys still waiting for baptism, so they would not die without it.
Then they were marched to Namugongo, and there they were burned. Tradition remembers that they went praying, some of them singing. A boy named Kizito is remembered holding Lwanga's hand.
Third, together. Anglican Christians at court died too, in the same persecution, for the same refusal.
The Catholic Church has canonized Charles Lwanga and his Catholic companions, and the Church of Uganda honors its Anglican martyrs.
At Namugongo there are two shrines, one Catholic and one Anglican, and pilgrims come to both.
Fourth, the word martyr. It comes from the Greek for witness: someone whose life, and death, tells the truth about what they believe.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THEY THAT SUFFER PERSECUTION.
teach.b: Jesus says in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Look back over this week: a doctrine that grows, a broom in the corner, we lepers, a nurse who stayed, a priest on a rope, a pope on wages, and now young men from two churches walking the same road to Namugongo.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Charles Lwanga and companions on June 3, and on that day pilgrims from Uganda and neighboring countries gather at the Catholic and Anglican shrines at Namugongo.

games.q: you lead the young Christian pages. the king's anger is growing, and some of the boys are still waiting for baptism. what do you do?
o: tell them to hide their faith until it's safe.
games.why: tradition says Charles Lwanga baptized them the night before they were taken to Namugongo.

practice: Picture Namugongo today: two shrines, crowds of pilgrims walking the roads to get there. Think of the people of Uganda now, families, schools, churches of more than one kind, people of other faiths and of none.
If you pray, pray for the country and its people; if you don't, hold them in mind with good will.
